title: Silk Road Camel Bells
note: SUT-facing prompt stream. Read segments in order; no labels are provided by design.

segments.prompt: At dusk, caravan master Shen Yan（A caravan master in his thirties, short full beard, turmeric headscarf, dark-brown leather coat, a copper steelyard weight at his waist, sharp eyes） lifts the curtain out of the sand dust into the inn hall（The open hall of a rammed-earth inn, oil lamps hung from the beams, felt rugs on the floor, salt bags and hides stacked along the wall）, bronze-lion sealing stamp（A palm-sized bronze sealing stamp with a lion knob, mane lines clear, face carved with the two characters Shen Ji, sealing wax bright red and uncracked） clutched in his palm.
A row of five tallow oil lamps（A row of five pottery tallow oil lamps hung under the inn-hall beams, shades wiped clear） hangs under the inn-hall beams; Shen Yan wipes each shade clean with a cloth.
Two bronze camel bells（Two bronze camel bells hanging by the inn eaves, bodies green with rust, low chime when the wind rises） hang by the inn eaves; Shen Yan reaches out and lets them touch lightly.
Shen Yan presses the bronze-lion sealing stamp into softened sealing wax; the two characters Shen Ji rise in the red wax.
He leans on a salt bag listening to the camel-bell aftertone, lamplight flickering on his short beard.

Shen Yan unties the camel-hair cord and opens the sheepskin-covered camel-bell ledger（A camel-bell ledger bound in sheepskin, tied with camel-hair cord, pages recording fodder and freight rates in vermilion ink）.
In vermilion ink he columns fodder weights, freight rates, and tomorrow's water stops.
Shen Yan closes the ledger and sets the bronze-lion sealing stamp beside the sheepskin cord.

On the dune yard（Rolling dunes outside the inn; sunset stretches the caravan silhouette long, wind lifting fine sand） at dawn, Shen Yan greets young Xiao He（A lean camel-hand girl of fourteen or fifteen, indigo sash, a small copper bell on her left ear, bright stubborn eyes） leading Crescent（A fat two-humped camel with a crescent brand on one hump, a bronze bell at her nose, laden with heavy salt bags） the camel.
Xiao He pats Crescent's neck; the nose bronze bell jingles.

Shen Yan points to the cowrie coin string（Three sea-cowrie coins strung on a red cord, faces polished bright, hanging from an inn beam） on the inn beam—three sea cowries clicking lightly on the red cord—and teaches Xiao He to judge their quality.
Xiao He crouches at the dune edge and traces the crescent brand on Crescent's hump with a finger.

In the poplar alley（A narrow alley of poplar wood inside the pass town, heavy shadow, plaster peeling to show wheat straw）, Aying（A youth whose face and build closely match Xiao He's, but wearing a silver-gray armband, no bell on the right ear, expression dark and swaggering） in a silver-gray armband glances back from behind the wall shadow.
Aying knocks the adobe wall with his knuckles, right ear bare, expression dark.
Aying carries an empty salt bag through the far end of the poplar alley.
On the dune yard, Xiao He and Aying brush past—one in an indigo sash, one in a silver-gray armband.
Xiao He guards the copper bell on her left ear; Aying glimpses the bell glint, presses his mouth, and skirts the camel shadow.
The two part at a dune fork, each walking opposite ways.
Months later on a sandstorm night, Shen Yan keeps watch alone in the inn hall, bronze-lion sealing stamp on his knee.

Shen Yan opens the camel-bell ledger（The same camel-bell ledger with yellow sand packed into the spine, cover wrinkled, vermilion ink bled into brown blotches）; the cover is wrinkled with packed yellow sand, vermilion ink blurred into brown blotches.
Shen Yan blows fine sand from the seams of the bronze-lion sealing stamp, face grave.
Through the long sand season, Shen Yan spreads camel tags by route and checks each freight rate.
Another snowy night, he wraps his leather coat tight and dries soaked reins by the oil lamp.
In spring flood season, Shen Yan stands at the felt curtain mouth, listening first for distant camel bells before counting returning silhouettes.
At high summer noon, Shen Yan moves the salt bags to the shady side of the inn.
In autumn sand haze, he brushes grit from the bronze lion-knob mane lines with a fine brush.
Another New Year's Eve, Shen Yan lines water skins by the door and keeps the inn alone until dawn.
At daybreak Shen Yan patrols the dune yard; Crescent the camel lies by the salt bags.
Shen Yan crouches to check whether Crescent's horseshoes are loose.
Shen Yan rebinds the spilled salt bags and pats yellow sand from his cuffs.

An ash-gray pack donkey（An ash-gray pack donkey with brand-new saddle pads but no crescent brand, nothing like Crescent the camel） turns out from behind a dune, saddle pads brand-new but no crescent brand.
A sandstorm rises suddenly; the inn felt curtain beats the doorframe, and the bronze-lion sealing stamp on the table rolls toward the edge.

In a thunder-like wind howl, a crack bursts across the face of the bronze-lion sealing stamp（The same bronze-lion sealing stamp, mane lines worn bald by sand, a crack across the face, sealing wax mottled and flaking）.
On the dune, Crescent the camel staggers and kneels in the gale.

Crescent（Crescent the camel kneels dead in a sand pit, crescent brand still clear, nose bell askew, salt bags spilled open） finally dies in the sand pit, nose bronze bell askew, salt bags spilled open.
Shen Yan lunges for the cracked bronze-lion sealing stamp and clutches it hard in his palm.
The day after the sandstorm, Shen Yan stands in the inn hall, thumb slowly tracing the crack of the bronze-lion sealing stamp.
Beside a blank page of the camel-bell ledger Shen Yan sketches the askew nose bronze bell and marks the date Crescent died.
Crescent's worn-white old rein hangs by the wall; Shen Yan retightens the knot.
He takes down one of the five tallow oil lamps from the beam and sits alone in the faint light.
At the end of the salt-bag list Shen Yan adds Crescent's load; the vermilion ink trembles as he writes.
Weeks later Shen Yan brings a pass-town copper smith and buries the cracked stamp in charcoal ash to preheat.

The smith takes out a fake lion stamp（A half-palm fake lion-knob stamp, shape close to the bronze-lion sealing stamp, but no Shen Ji on the face and blurry mane lines） as a calibration mold—it looks like the real one but has no Shen Ji characters.

Molten copper seeps along the crack and is filed smooth; the bronze-lion sealing stamp（New bronze has been cast into the crack of the bronze-lion sealing stamp; mane lines a little shallower, Shen Ji still readable, sealing wax freshly reddened） is usable again, mane lines a little shallower.
While the bronze stamp is still warm, Shen Yan burns a bright-red seal onto the back of a transit wooden tag.

A wooden-wheel cart（A creaking wooden-wheel cart loaded with clay jars, not salt bags—nothing like the caravan's Crescent） creaks into the dune yard loaded with clay jars, nothing to do with the already-dead Crescent.

The checkpoint tax officer（A lean checkpoint tax officer also in a turmeric headscarf and brown leather coat, but with an official-seal pouch on the shoulder, build close to Shen Yan's） jumps down the dune and talks shoulder to shoulder with Shen Yan; both wear turmeric headscarves.
The tax officer checks jar duty on a wooden tag; Shen Yan registers it in a separate column from salt-bag freight rates.

A Cuier（A tea-shed serving girl from the pass town, light-brown sash; at a glance much like young Xiao He, but with a bell on the right ear and shy unfamiliar eyes） in a light-brown sash arrives from the pass-town tea shed; at a glance she looks somewhat like young Xiao He.
Cuier tries to tie a camel rein, but Shen Yan shakes his head—she wears a bell on the right ear; she is not Xiao He after all.

Years later at dusk, limping Shen Yan（The same Shen Yan: headscarf torn by grit, left leg wrapped in hemp cloth, limping on a broken spear haft, coat crusted with blood scabs and sand） leans on a broken spear haft under the abandoned pass fort（A half-collapsed loess pass fort, empty gate tunnel, feather grass on the battlements, wind moaning） gate tunnel.
Those two bronze camel bells under the abandoned pass fort eaves chime lightly in the wind; Shen Yan stops to listen.
Shen Yan presses his palm to the cold loess wall of the fort, as if saying goodbye.

By day, adult Xiao He（A woman master in her twenties, still wearing the indigo sash and left-ear copper bell, upright bearing, steady eyes） returns along the sand track and hurries toward the abandoned pass fort.
Xiao He reunites with limping Shen Yan under the fort; they embrace.
By the fort kang, Xiao He holds Shen Yan's withered hand.
Shen Yan（Shen Yan lies still on the pass-town kang with eyes closed, leather coat covering his chest, no breath left）'s breath fades; at last he closes his eyes and dies at the pass.
Shen Yan's old dark-brown leather coat still hangs behind the fort gate; Xiao He brushes sand from the shoulder.
By the inn doorpost, adult Xiao He straightens the slanted Shen brass plaque（A brass nameplate nailed to the inn doorpost, carved with Shen Caravan and the founding year, edges green with verdigris）.
Xiao He picks verdigris from the plaque letter grooves with a fingernail; Shen Yan's name shines again.

Disguised Aying（After a change of look Aying still wears the silver-gray armband; a new sand scar on the brow, expression deeper） arrives from outside the fort and locks eyes with Xiao He under the gate tunnel.
Xiao He and Aying stand side by side under the abandoned pass fort—one calm, one brooding.
The sand curtain rolls back years—that youth tracing a hump brand at the dune edge is outlined again by morning light.
Old firelight in the inn hall flares again; a bronze-lion sealing stamp is pressed into red wax for the first time.
Wind lifts the shadow of the poplar alley; that figure in a silver-gray armband with a bare right ear skims past the wall base.
In dim yellow lamplight, that row of five pottery tallow lamps under the inn beams lines up again.
The rolling dunes of first meeting spread again; wind lifts fine sand, camel shadows slowly approach from afar.
Xiao He carries the sand-stained blurred camel-bell ledger across the inn-hall threshold.
Those five tallow oil lamps under the inn beams still burn; Xiao He checks them east to west in order.
On the wooden beam, those three cowrie coins on the string still hang in place.
Xiao He grips the recast bronze-lion sealing stamp and passes a new caravan tag to the westbound line.
